transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you’re here. What brings you in today?

Oh, hello. Thank you. Well, I came in because... oh, it’s just gotten to be too much, and I don't know what's wrong with me. I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It’s like my brain just freezes up completely. 

For example, if you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table... well, it's just a disaster. It’s completely covered. You can't even see the wood underneath, which is a shame because it's a lovely oak table we bought years ago, but right now it is just buried. It's covered with my husband’s appointment papers—he has the cardiologist and the podiatrist, and keeping track of all those little reminder cards they hand you is a job in itself. And then mixed in with all of his things, I have all these church flyers for the bake sale and the prayer group, and notes they hand out at the senior center, and... oh, just piles of half-finished lists. I try to make lists to keep it all straight, I really do, but I never seem to finish writing them. 

So I'll make a cup of tea in the morning and sit down at that table, intending to finally sort it all out, and I just... I sit there. I look at the medical bills, and then the church bulletins, and then my little scraps of paper, and I just don't know which thing to do first. I stare at it all, and my mind just spins, and I sit there paralyzed until the whole day is gone. The tea gets ice cold, the sun goes down, and I haven't accomplished a single thing. It's happening every single day, and I just feel so foolish at my age not being able to handle a simple stack of mail.
Do you often need other people to make decisions for you, even simple everyday ones?

Oh, goodness, no, it’s not that at all. I don’t need anyone to decide things for me. I know perfectly well what I want or what needs to be done. Like with my husband—he's always asking me what we should have for dinner, or which route we should take to his cardiologist appointments because of all that awful construction on the interstate, and I have absolutely no trouble telling him exactly what we are going to do. I can make a decision just fine. I've always been very independent in my thinking, really ever since my college days when I had to put together my own course schedules and manage my own affairs. 

So the problem isn't the deciding part. It’s... well, it's the doing part. I'll decide that I am going to sit down and pay the electric bill, and I know exactly which checkbook to use—the blue one with the little sailboats on it that we got from the credit union years ago—and I know it needs a stamp, and I know exactly where the stamps are kept in the top left drawer. But I just can't seem to make myself actually do the steps. I just get stuck after the decision is already made. So, no, I certainly don't go around asking people to choose things for me or run my life. I’m not helpless in that way, I just... I get trapped in the execution of it all, if that makes any sense.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most days lately?

Oh, sad? Hopeless? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Frustrated, certainly. I get so terribly frustrated with myself I could just scream sometimes, but it’s not the same as being depressed or hopeless. I still very much look forward to things. 

Like, in the mornings, I'll wake up and open the blinds—we have these lovely heavy curtains in the bedroom because the streetlamp outside our window is just blindingly bright at night, but once I pull them back, the morning light is just beautiful. And I'll stand there and think to myself about all the wonderful things I want to do that day. I want to go to my prayer group, I want to bake my lemon squares for the church bake sale... I still use the recipe my mother gave me, the one that uses real lemon zest, not that bottled extract nonsense you buy at the grocery store. 

So the desire is absolutely there, and the hope is there! I love my life, and I love my husband, even if his medical paperwork is taking over my beautiful oak table. It’s just that when I actually go to *do* the things I’m so looking forward to, I get stuck. But I'm not sitting around crying or feeling down in the dumps like... well, like some of the ladies I know at the senior center who just seem to have given up on things. My friend Martha, for instance, she gets very blue, won't even leave her recliner for days on end, just watches the television with the volume turned all the way up. I'm not like that at all. I have plenty of hope and plenty of things I want to do. I just... I just can't seem to get my gears to catch, if you know what I mean. But no, I'm not sad or hopeless most days. Just terribly, terribly annoyed with my own brain.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. Not at all. Like I was just saying, I still want to do all those things. I still absolutely love the idea of them. Take my gardening, for instance. I've always loved tending to my flower beds. We have these beautiful hydrangea bushes along the side of the house—the big mophead kind, you know? And I know exactly what they need right now. They need to be deadheaded, and the soil needs a little bit of that acidic fertilizer to keep the blooms nice and blue, because if you let the soil get too alkaline, they turn this washed-out pink color that I just don't care for at all. 

So I still get excited about it, and I'll buy the fertilizer at the garden center, and I'll set it right there by the back door, fully intending to go out there and spend a lovely afternoon in the dirt. The interest is completely there! I want to see those beautiful blue flowers just as much as I ever did. But then... well, I'll look at the fertilizer bag, and then I'll think about getting my gardening gloves, which are somewhere in the garage, probably behind my husband's old golf clubs that he hasn't used since his knee surgery in 2018. And then I think about having to move the clubs, and then I just... I freeze up again. 

So the bag of fertilizer just sits there by the door for weeks. Every time I walk past it, I think, "Oh, I really want to do that," but I just can't make myself start the process. It's not that I don't care anymore, or that I wouldn't enjoy it if I could just get out there. I know I would! I love the smell of the damp earth and the feeling of the sun on my back. The pleasure of it hasn't gone away one bit. It's just the... the getting to it that stops me cold. So no, the interest is definitely still there, it's just trapped behind whatever it is that's keeping me from actually doing anything.
Do you find it hard to do things on your own unless someone else reassures or encourages you?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Reassurance? No, I don't need anyone to pat me on the back or tell me I'm doing the right thing. Like I said before, I'm very independent in my thinking. I know what needs to be done. 

Take my husband's medication schedule, for instance. He has so many pills now—the blood pressure ones, the cholesterol ones, the blood thinners, and those little water pills that make him have to run to the restroom every hour on the hour. It's a whole production, really. I bought one of those big plastic organizers, the ones with the days of the week in big bold letters and little separate compartments for morning, noon, and night. I know exactly how to fill it, and I don't need him or anyone else standing over my shoulder telling me, "Oh, good job, dear, you put the blue pill in the right slot." I know where the blue pill goes! 

I don't need encouragement to start a task, I just... well, the problem is starting it, yes, but it's not for a lack of encouragement. If I need to sort his pills, I know I need to do it, and I'll look at all the bottles lined up on the kitchen counter—right next to the toaster, which I really need to clean, the crumbs are just getting everywhere—and I'll think, "Okay, time to sort the pills." But then I'll just stand there staring at them. It's not that I'm waiting for someone to cheer me on. I don't feel unsure of myself. I just... I can't make my hands reach out and open the bottles. 

So, no, I certainly don't rely on other people to coax me into doing things. I'm a grown woman, I've run a household for forty-five years. I don't need a cheerleader, I just need my brain to let me do the things I already know I need to do!
Do you usually have difficulty expressing disagreement with other people, even when you think they may be wrong?

Oh, heavens no. I have absolutely no trouble speaking my mind if I think someone is wrong. Never have, really. My mother used to say I had a tongue like a pair of pinking shears—always ready to trim the fray! I just don't see the point in sitting quietly if someone is making a mistake or saying something foolish. 

Take my book club, for example. We meet every second Tuesday of the month at the library, in that little glass-walled room they added on during the renovation back in 2015. Well, last month, Susan—she's the one who always brings those dry, store-bought cookies instead of baking something herself, which I just don't understand because baking is so simple if you just follow the recipe—anyway, Susan was going on and on about how the protagonist in the novel we were reading was acting completely out of character in the final chapters. And she was just entirely wrong! She had completely missed the subtle foreshadowing in chapter four where the author described the protagonist's relationship with her estranged sister. 

Well, I certainly didn't just sit there and nod along to keep the peace. I spoke right up. I said, "Susan, dear, I think you've missed the entire point of the sister's subplot." And I laid it all out for her, chapter and verse. Some of the other ladies looked a bit uncomfortable—you know how people get when there's a disagreement, they start shifting in their chairs and looking at their watches—but I don't mind that at all. If you're going to discuss a book, you should discuss it properly, not just agree with whatever nonsense the loudest person in the room is spouting. 

And it's the same with the doctors, no offense to you, of course! But when my husband's cardiologist tried to tell me that his new diet didn't need to be strictly low-sodium, I marched right up to that front desk and demanded a printout of the latest guidelines, because I had read an article in a medical journal—I still have my library card, and I use the online databases, which took me forever to figure out how to log into, but I did it—and I knew the doctor was working off old information. I told him so, too! 

So no, I don't have any difficulty disagreeing with people. If I think I'm right, or if I know someone else is wrong, I will absolutely say so. I don't need to hide my opinions just to make other people comfortable. My problem isn't speaking up... it's just getting myself to do the things I speak up about!
Have you been having trouble remembering recent events or information, like appointments, conversations, or where you put things?

Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, I have. It's... well, it's becoming quite a nuisance, to be perfectly honest with you. It feels like things just slip right through a sieve in my brain lately! 

Take the telephone, for instance. I’ve missed returning I don't even know how many calls. My sister called on Sunday to tell me all about her new patio furniture—wicker, with these lovely teal cushions that she found on sale—and I listened to the voicemail, fully intending to call her right back after I finished my cup of tea. But did I? No. It completely vanished from my mind until she called again on Wednesday asking if I was upset with her! 

And the mail... oh, the mail is just a disaster area. Gary, our postman, he drops it through the slot in the front door, and I'll scoop it up and set it on the little half-moon table in the foyer. I tell myself I'll sort it, but then it just sits there. Just last week, I realized I had left the water bill sitting under a massive stack of mail and catalogs—those clothing catalogs that I never even order from anymore because the sizing has gotten so terribly inconsistent. I had just left the bill sitting there, completely forgotten!

It happens with my family, too, which makes me feel just awful. I’ve forgotten errands I promised my daughter I’d do for her. She was so busy last week with her children's school plays, and I told her, "Don't you worry, I'll go to the craft store and get that special backing fabric you need." I promised her! And then... I just didn't. I completely forgot until she came over asking for it. 

But I think what bothers me the most is my husband’s schedule. I told you about his medications, but his doctors... they always want you to call and confirm the appointments, or they leave those automated messages where you have to call back. And more than once recently, I've realized way, way too late that I never actually confirmed one of his appointments. I'll get that sudden panic in my chest on the morning he's supposed to go, thinking, "Did I ever call that girl at the front desk back?" And usually, I haven't. The information comes in, and I just... I lose it entirely.
Have these memory and organization problems been getting noticeably worse over time?

Well, you see, it is not so much that it has just been a slow, invisible decline where I suddenly woke up and could not remember anything. I can actually pinpoint it quite specifically. It has been causing this level of absolute chaos for about a year and three months now. Yes, right around fifteen months. I know that because it was late winter last year, just after I finally got all the holiday decorations packed away into the attic, which always takes me weeks to finish anyway because I have to wrap each delicate ornament in its own specific piece of tissue paper. 

But anyway, a year and three months ago, that was exactly when my husband really started needing regular help with his appointments and all his daily arrangements. Before that, he mostly managed his own schedule. He would write his little reminders on the golf calendar we keep by the refrigerator. But then his needs changed, and suddenly I was the one who had to be the project manager for his entire life. Keeping track of the doctors, the pharmacy trips, the daily routines... it all fell squarely onto my shoulders. 

And that is when this trouble really became impossible to ignore. Because if I forget to drink my own cup of tea, it is just cold tea, but if I forget to manage his arrangements, it is a real disaster. I try to write things down on those little yellow sticky notes, but then the notes lose their stickiness and fall behind the telephone table, and then I am on my hands and knees looking for a piece of paper while he is asking what time we are supposed to leave. So yes, for the last year and three months, it has just been a terrible struggle to keep all these plates spinning, and I just feel like they are all crashing down around me.
Have these memory and organization problems started to interfere with your independence in daily life, such as managing finances, medications, or appointments without help?

Oh, it just breaks my heart to admit it, but... yes. Yes, it really has started to affect my independence, and I absolutely hate it. I have always prided myself on being a capable woman, you know. 

For years—oh, it must be going on a decade now—I was the one who organized the big annual charity auction at our local senior center. It is a massive undertaking, let me tell you, coordinating all the local businesses for donations, arranging the catering, making sure the tablecloths match the napkins, setting up the silent auction tables so there is good flow for the foot traffic. But this year... well, I had to completely give up leading the event. I just had to step down. I was misplacing the contact sheets, I could not remember which bakery had promised the dinner rolls, and the stress of trying to hold all those moving pieces in my head when they kept slipping away... I just could not do it anymore. I had to hand the whole binder over to someone else.

And it is not just the volunteer work, it is right here in my own home. My daughter, bless her, she means well, she really does. But she has started coming over every single weekend to double-check all of our bills and my husband's appointments. She will sit right there at my kitchen table with her laptop and go through everything I am supposed to have done for the week. It is humiliating, frankly. But after that water bill incident I told you about, and a few times where we almost missed the doctor, she just... well, she no longer trusts that I can keep everything straight on my own. 

She tells me she is just helping out, but I know what it really means. She does not think I can manage my own household affairs without supervision anymore. I try to organize the mail into little piles for paying and filing, but they all just blur together, and if she was not checking up on me, I honestly do not know what would happen to our electricity or my husband's checkups. So yes, I am losing my grip on doing things myself, and it is just an awful, awful feeling.
Do you have trouble handling basic self-care tasks like bathing, dressing, or eating without help?

Oh, heavens no. No, no, I am perfectly capable of taking care of my own personal hygiene and getting myself dressed, thank goodness. I haven't quite reached the point where I need a nursemaid for that! 

I still take my shower every single morning, right after I wake up. I have this lovely lavender body wash—my niece Sarah bought it for me from one of those fancy boutique shops downtown, the ones where everything costs an arm and a leg, but oh, it smells just divine, like a real English garden. I make sure I am washed and dressed properly every single day without anyone's assistance. I've always firmly believed that if you don't get out of your nightgown, the day is just entirely lost to you. So I always pick out a nice pair of slacks and a blouse. Sometimes it takes me a minute to decide which blouse, of course, because I have to make sure it matches my cardigan if there's a chill in the house, but I put it all on myself without a lick of trouble. 

And eating? Oh, I can feed myself just fine. I still do the cooking, even if I occasionally forget to take the chicken out of the freezer in time and we have to settle for sandwiches instead of a hot meal. But no, as far as physically bathing and putting on my clothes and eating my meals, I don't need anyone's help with that at all. I can manage my own body, thankfully, even if the paperwork and the schedules are driving me absolutely batty.
Have you ever had a stroke, head injury, or any other problem with your brain before these memory difficulties started?

No, no, thank goodness. Nothing like that at all. I have never had a stroke or a brain injury or anything of that dreadful sort. I've always been very healthy in that regard. 

Well, I did have a terrible bout of vertigo once, oh, it must have been in the late nineties. The room would just spin and spin every time I turned my head too quickly. It was awful, truly awful. I had to sleep propped up on three pillows for a fortnight. Dr. Miller—he was our physician back then, before he retired and moved to Florida, lovely man with the most calming bedside manner—he said it was an inner ear thing. But that wasn't my brain, you see. That was just my ears acting up. 

But as for actual brain problems, like a stroke? No, I've never had anything like that. My mother, rest her soul, she had a small stroke when she was eighty-two, and it affected her speech for a little while. She couldn't find the right words for things. She kept calling the refrigerator the "cold box," which we all thought was rather sweet, but it was very frightening at the time. So I know what that looks like, and I haven't had anything even remotely similar. 

I've never fallen and hit my head, either. I'm very careful about that. I always hold the handrail when I go down the stairs to the basement, even when I'm carrying a load of laundry, which is getting harder to do these days. I make sure to leave one hand free just for the rail. And I wear sensible shoes around the house, none of those slippery slippers that can send you flying across the linoleum. So no, my brain has never been injured or damaged in any physical way, it's just... well, it's just this dreadful fog and confusion with keeping everything organized lately. But physically? No, my brain has been perfectly fine.
Have these memory and thinking problems been steadily getting worse over time?

Well, I suppose... yes, I think they have been getting steadily worse, though it’s hard to put an exact finger on when it really started going downhill. It’s not like waking up one morning and suddenly everything is different, you know? It’s more like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it at first, but then one day you realize you're driving on the rim. 

I mean, I look back to maybe five or six years ago, and I was still juggling so many things. I’d have the church bake sale on a Tuesday, my book club on Thursday, and I’d still manage to remember to send out all the grandchildren’s birthday cards right on time, with a crisp five-dollar bill tucked inside. But then, little by little, the edges started fraying. First, it was just walking into a room and forgetting why I went in there, which everyone does, right? I used to joke with my neighbor, Susan—she lives in the blue house at the end of the cul-de-sac, lovely woman, makes the most incredible rhubarb pie—I used to joke with her that my brain was just too full of recipes and old phone numbers to fit anything new. 

But then it wasn't a joke anymore. It progressed from forgetting why I went into the kitchen to forgetting to pay the electric bill for two months in a row. And then the auction incident I told you about... that was the real wake-up call. It just feels like every year, every month even, the fog gets a little thicker. The pile of mail on the counter gets a little higher because I just can't sort through it as quickly as I used to. The effort it takes to just figure out what day it is and what I’m supposed to be doing... it’s exhausting. 

So yes, to answer your question, it definitely hasn't stayed the same. It’s been a slow, steady, creeping sort of decline, and it just terrifies me to think about where I’ll be next year if it keeps going at this rate. I used to be sharp as a tack, Doctor, I really was. And now... now I just feel like I'm slowly losing pieces of myself, one forgotten appointment at a time.
How old were you when these memory and thinking problems first started?

Well, see, that's the thing. You ask when they *first* started, and... well, it's not quite as simple as saying it all began five years ago when I started messing up the bills. Because, honestly? If I really think back on it, if I'm being perfectly truthful... I've always been this way. Always. 

It's just that it's gotten so much harder to manage now that I'm older, but the foundation of it? Oh, it's been there my whole life. I mean, even as a little girl, way back in grade school at St. Mary's—Sister Margaret was my third-grade teacher, she was so strict, she used a wooden ruler to point at the chalkboard, and you did *not* want to be on the wrong end of that ruler—but even back then, my report cards always said the exact same thing. Every single term. My mother used to sigh so heavily when she read them. They'd write that I was a bright girl, very capable, but that I was just terribly careless. 

I was always forgetting my textbooks at school, or leaving my homework on the kitchen table after I'd spent all evening struggling to get it done. And oh, the daydreaming! I'd just drift off, staring out the window at the playground, and Sister Margaret would have to rap her knuckles on my desk to bring me back. I always needed constant reminders just to finish my seatwork. The other children would be done and lining up for recess, and I'd still be staring at the same math problem, my mind a million miles away, and they'd have to tell me I couldn't go outside until I finished. 

So, you see, it’s not a new thing, not really. It’s just that when you're young, people call you a daydreamer or say you're not applying yourself. And then you grow up and you find little ways to cope, little systems. You write things down, you make piles, you try so hard to keep the plates spinning. But now... now I'm seventy, and I just don't have the energy to keep those plates spinning anymore, and they're all crashing down. But the trouble with focusing and remembering what I'm supposed to be doing? That's been with me since I was a little girl in pigtails.
When you were a child, before these memory problems now, did teachers or family ever say you had trouble paying attention or were easily distracted?

Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying! I suppose I jumped the gun a little bit on your questions, didn't I? I do apologize, sometimes my mouth just runs right ahead of the rest of me and I get carried away with my own stories. But yes, absolutely, they did. Like I was telling you about Sister Margaret and the others, even as a little girl, my teachers always wrote those exact same notes home to my parents. They would write that I was a bright child, which was nice of them to say, I suppose, but they always, always followed it up by saying I was terribly careless. 

My mother would get so frustrated, bless her heart, because I was constantly forgetting my books at school. Or I would actually manage to do my homework—sitting there for hours at our old yellow formica kitchen table, rubbing my eyes and trying so hard to get it done—and then I would just leave it sitting right there on the table the next morning when I went to catch the bus. 

And the attention part... oh, it was just dreadful. I was so easily distracted by every little thing, a bird outside, a squeaky chair, you name it. I constantly needed reminders just to finish my daily seatwork. The teachers would have to come over, tap on my desk, and tell me I couldn't go outside until I finished my work. I can still picture it, all the other children running out the door for recess, laughing and shouting, and I'd still be sitting there all alone in the quiet classroom, trying to force my brain to just focus on the page in front of me. So, yes, long before any of these current issues with my bills and the mail, everyone always told me I had trouble paying attention.
Has your memory or thinking gotten worse over the last few years, or has it stayed about the same since childhood?

Well, I know I’m throwing a lot of different timelines at you, and I do apologize if I'm making a muddle of things. It’s just... well, it’s both, really. The tendency to lose focus and drift off, that foundation has been there since childhood, exactly like I said. But the actual severity of it? Oh, it has absolutely gotten worse over the last few years. 

But if I have to pinpoint exactly when it went from just being a slow, frustrating decline to... to this awful state where I'm missing bills and feeling completely underwater? It has been causing *this* much trouble for about a year and three months. 

That was right around the time my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and his daily arrangements. He’s always been the organized one, you see, the one who kept the calendar straight. But he started needing me to step in and manage his schedule for him. Suddenly, I wasn't just trying to keep my own scattered thoughts in order, I had to keep track of when he needed to be at the clinic, organizing his transportation, making sure his days were structured and everything was running smoothly for him. 

And it was just... it was just too much for my brain to handle. I was barely keeping my own head above water as it was, and adding his schedule to my plate just broke whatever little coping systems I had left. It's like I was already carrying an armful of groceries and someone tossed a watermelon on top. So, yes, while I've always been this way deep down, this current level of trouble, where everything is just completely falling apart on me, that really took hold about fifteen months ago when I had to take over his arrangements.
When you were younger, before all of these recent memory concerns, did you already have trouble keeping organized or following through on tasks?

Well, yes, I suppose I did always struggle with keeping things neat and following through. Even back when I was younger, taking a few college classes, my binders were always a jumble and I'd start a project with all the enthusiasm in the world and then just sort of... fizzle out. But I could usually scrape by back then. 

But now? Well, the real reason I finally came in to see you—the thing that made me realize I need help—is because I just can’t seem to get *anything* in order anymore. It's reached a point where it's completely unmanageable. 

If you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table... oh my goodness, it's just a disaster. It is completely covered, edge to edge, just a sea of paper. I've got my husband’s appointment papers stacked up everywhere—because, like I was telling you, I have to keep track of all his doctors and transport now—and then mixed right in with those are the church flyers, because I try to stay involved with the congregation, and then there are all these senior-center notes... 

And I try to make lists, I really do! I think to myself, "Okay, I'll just write it all down and tackle it one by one," but then I just end up with all these half-finished lists scattered across the table, too. Written on the backs of envelopes, on little tear-off pads... And I'll make a cup of tea, and I'll sit down at that table, and I just... I sit there not knowing which thing to do first. Should I call the clinic? Should I sort the church bulletin? Should I finish the grocery list? I just stare at it all, feeling so incredibly overwhelmed, and I shuffle the papers around, and before I know it, the whole day is gone. The sun is setting, the tea is cold, and I haven't actually accomplished a single thing. It's just an awful, awful feeling to lose your whole day to a pile of paper.
When you are doing something you really enjoy, can you focus on it for a long time?

Well, now that's a very good question, and honestly, I'm not entirely sure how to answer it. I mean, what do I even really enjoy doing these days? It feels like all my time is just swallowed up by the appointments and the paperwork and trying to keep my head above water, like I was saying. 

I suppose... well, I used to love gardening. Oh, my roses were just beautiful! I had these lovely pink climbing roses that would go right up the trellis by the back porch. I'd spend hours out there, pruning and weeding, getting my hands dirty. I'd put on my big straw hat and my old canvas gloves—the ones with the little green flowers on them, you know the kind?—and I'd just lose myself in it. I'd go out there after breakfast and the next thing I knew, my husband would be calling out the back door that it was time for lunch. 

But lately? Even if I did have the time, between the senior center and the church and the clinic schedules, I just don't know if I could stick with it like I used to. I try to read sometimes, I've always loved a good mystery novel, Agatha Christie and the like. I'll sit down in my favorite armchair—the floral one by the window where the light is good—and I'll open the book, and I'll read a page or two... but then I find myself thinking about whether I remembered to call the transport service for Tuesday, or if I paid the electric bill, or I'll just hear a car go by outside and my mind just completely wanders away from the story. I'll read the same paragraph three times and still not know what happened. 

So, I suppose I don't really know if I can focus on things I enjoy anymore, because it feels like it's been so long since I've been able to just sit down and truly enjoy something without my mind buzzing off in a hundred different directions. It's just so frustrating, it really is. It makes me feel like I'm losing pieces of myself, you know? The parts that used to be able to just relax and enjoy a beautiful afternoon.
Before adulthood, did you already have trouble paying attention or keeping organized?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It goes all the way back, it really does. I know I mentioned struggling a bit in those few college classes I took, but if we're talking about long before that, before adulthood... well, even as a little girl in grade school, it was the exact same story. 

I actually still remember those old report cards. My mother used to keep them in a cedar box in the hall closet—she kept absolutely everything, you see, which is probably where I get my terrible habit of keeping all these papers on the kitchen table! But I remember looking at those report cards years later, and it seemed like every single year, the teachers always wrote the exact same things in the margins. 

I remember Mrs. Gable, my third-grade teacher—she had this beautiful, sweeping cursive handwriting—and she wrote that I was a very bright girl, but oh, so careless. "Bright but careless," that was the phrase that just seemed to follow me everywhere I went. I was always, always forgetting my reading books at school, or I'd leave my homework sitting right there on the kitchen counter after I'd spent the whole evening agonizing over it with my father. 

And the daydreaming! I'd just sit at my little wooden desk, staring out the window at the playground, watching the older children or just looking at the clouds rolling by, and I just wouldn't get my work done. The teachers were constantly having to come over, tap on my desk, and give me reminders. They'd say, "Now, you need to finish your seatwork before you can go outside for recess," and I'd suddenly snap out of it and panic because I hadn't even written my name at the top of the page yet, and all the other children were already lining up at the door. So, yes, that trouble paying attention and keeping my things straight... that's been a part of me since I was just a tiny thing in pigtails, long before I ever had to worry about clinic schedules or bills.
When you were a child, did teachers or family ever say you had trouble paying attention or were easily distracted?

Well, yes, like I was just saying about the daydreaming and Mrs. Gable, my family and teachers were always bringing it up. My mother used to sigh and tell my father that I was just living in my own little world, completely distracted by the dust motes in the air. 

But you know, the frustrating part is that it never really went away. If anything, it feels like it's so much worse now that I have all these important things to manage. Just the other day, I was trying to sit down and figure out the schedule for the week—which, let me tell you, is practically a full-time job with all the different transport vans and pickup times for my husband—and he had the television on in the next room. It wasn't even loud, just that low murmur of the afternoon news, but my mind just latched right onto it. 

Or, oh, it happens all the time at the senior center, too! I'll be sitting at one of those folding tables in the rec room, trying to jot down some notes for the upcoming bake sale or organize the volunteer list, and if two people sit down anywhere near me and start talking... well, that's the end of my productivity right there. They could be talking about absolutely anything—the weather, their grandchildren, the price of eggs at the supermarket—and my mind just completely leaves what I'm doing and follows their conversation instead. I just can't seem to filter it out, no matter how hard I try. 

I'll be sitting there with my pen hovering over the paper, and suddenly I realize I've been eavesdropping on Margaret's kitchen renovation for ten minutes, and I look down and I've completely lost my place in what I was writing or planning. I won't even remember what I was trying to figure out in the first place! It's like my brain just packs up and walks away the second there's another noise. And then I have to start the whole planning process all over again, which just adds to that terrible pile of half-finished lists on my table. It’s just exhausting, having your attention hijacked by every little sound in the room.
Did you have these attention and organization problems already as a child?

Well, yes, like I was saying just a few minutes ago... I suppose we might be going over the same ground a bit, but yes, absolutely. Even as a little girl, it was always a problem. I know I mentioned those old report cards my mother kept in her cedar closet, but it really is striking when I think back on it. 

Every single year, my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless. That was the word they just loved to use, "careless." It used to just break my heart because I really wasn't trying to be! But I was always, always forgetting my reading books at school, or I'd spend the entire evening doing my homework with my father, only to just leave it sitting right on the kitchen counter the next morning. 

And getting my actual work done in the classroom was just a monumental task. I always needed extra reminders from the teachers to finish my seatwork before I could go outside. I'd just be sitting there at my desk, completely lost in my own thoughts or watching the clouds, and suddenly I'd realize all the other children were getting their coats on and heading out the door for recess, and I hadn't even started my assignment. So, yes, long before I was an adult, long before any of these modern worries, these exact same problems were right there with me.

patient.answer:
Oh, sad? Hopeless? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Frustrated, certainly. I get so terribly frustrated with myself I could just scream sometimes, but it’s not the same as being depressed or hopeless. I still very much look forward to things. 

Like, in the mornings, I'll wake up and open the blinds—we have these lovely heavy curtains in the bedroom because the streetlamp outside our window is just blindingly bright at night, but once I pull them back, the morning light is just beautiful. And I'll stand there and think to myself about all the wonderful things I want to do that day. I want to go to my prayer group, I want to bake my lemon squares for the church bake sale... I still use the recipe my mother gave me, the one that uses real lemon zest, not that bottled extract nonsense you buy at the grocery store. 

So the desire is absolutely there, and the hope is there! I love my life, and I love my husband, even if his medical paperwork is taking over my beautiful oak table. It’s just that when I actually go to *do* the things I’m so looking forward to, I get stuck. But I'm not sitting around crying or feeling down in the dumps like... well, like some of the ladies I know at the senior center who just seem to have given up on things. My friend Martha, for instance, she gets very blue, won't even leave her recliner for days on end, just watches the television with the volume turned all the way up. I'm not like that at all. I have plenty of hope and plenty of things I want to do. I just... I just can't seem to get my gears to catch, if you know what I mean. But no, I'm not sad or hopeless most days. Just terribly, terribly annoyed with my own brain.

doctor.intent: To distinguish depressive disorder from anxiety or dependent personality disorder by assessing for a key depressive symptom: loss of interest or pleasure.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure), which is a symptom of depression. My profile only contains symptoms of ADHD.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. Not at all. Like I was just saying, I still want to do all those things. I still absolutely love the idea of them. Take my gardening, for instance. I've always loved tending to my flower beds. We have these beautiful hydrangea bushes along the side of the house—the big mophead kind, you know? And I know exactly what they need right now. They need to be deadheaded, and the soil needs a little bit of that acidic fertilizer to keep the blooms nice and blue, because if you let the soil get too alkaline, they turn this washed-out pink color that I just don't care for at all. 

So I still get excited about it, and I'll buy the fertilizer at the garden center, and I'll set it right there by the back door, fully intending to go out there and spend a lovely afternoon in the dirt. The interest is completely there! I want to see those beautiful blue flowers just as much as I ever did. But then... well, I'll look at the fertilizer bag, and then I'll think about getting my gardening gloves, which are somewhere in the garage, probably behind my husband's old golf clubs that he hasn't used since his knee surgery in 2018. And then I think about having to move the clubs, and then I just... I freeze up again. 

So the bag of fertilizer just sits there by the door for weeks. Every time I walk past it, I think, "Oh, I really want to do that," but I just can't make myself start the process. It's not that I don't care anymore, or that I wouldn't enjoy it if I could just get out there. I know I would! I love the smell of the damp earth and the feeling of the sun on my back. The pleasure of it hasn't gone away one bit. It's just the... the getting to it that stops me cold. So no, the interest is definitely still there, it's just trapped behind whatever it is that's keeping me from actually doing anything.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Reassurance? No, I don't need anyone to pat me on the back or tell me I'm doing the right thing. Like I said before, I'm very independent in my thinking. I know what needs to be done. 

Take my husband's medication schedule, for instance. He has so many pills now—the blood pressure ones, the cholesterol ones, the blood thinners, and those little water pills that make him have to run to the restroom every hour on the hour. It's a whole production, really. I bought one of those big plastic organizers, the ones with the days of the week in big bold letters and little separate compartments for morning, noon, and night. So, no, I certainly don't rely on other people to coax me into doing things. I'm a grown woman, I've run a household for forty-five years. I don't need a cheerleader, I just need my brain to let me do the things I already know I need to do!

doctor.intent: To determine whether there is a pervasive pattern of submissive, dependent behavior that would support dependent personality disorder rather than depression, anxiety, or an unspecified cognitive problem.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens no. I have absolutely no trouble speaking my mind if I think someone is wrong. Never have, really. My mother used to say I had a tongue like a pair of pinking shears—always ready to trim the fray! I just don't see the point in sitting quietly if someone is making a mistake or saying something foolish. 

Take my book club, for example. We meet every second Tuesday of the month at the library, in that little glass-walled room they added on during the renovation back in 2015. Well, last month, Susan—she's the one who always brings those dry, store-bought cookies instead of baking something herself, which I just don't understand because baking is so simple if you just follow the recipe—anyway, Susan was going on and on about how the protagonist in the novel we were reading was acting completely out of character in the final chapters. And she was just entirely wrong! She had completely missed the subtle foreshadowing in chapter four where the author described the protagonist's relationship with her estranged sister. 

Well, I certainly didn't just sit there and nod along to keep the peace. I spoke right up. I said, "Susan, dear, I think you've missed the entire point of the sister's subplot." And I laid it all out for her, chapter and verse. Some of the other ladies looked a bit uncomfortable—you know how people get when there's a disagreement, they start shifting in their chairs and looking at their watches—but I don't mind that at all. If you're going to discuss a book, you should discuss it properly, not just agree with whatever nonsense the loudest person in the room is spouting. 

And it's the same with the doctors, no offense to you, of course! But when my husband's cardiologist tried to tell me that his new diet didn't need to be strictly low-sodium, I marched right up to that front desk and demanded a printout of the latest guidelines, because I had read an article in a medical journal—I still have my library card, and I use the online databases, which took me forever to figure out how to log into, but I did it—and I knew the doctor was working off old information. I told him so, too! 

So no, I don't have any difficulty disagreeing with people. If I think I'm right, or if I know someone else is wrong, I will absolutely say so. My sister called on Sunday to tell me all about her new patio furniture—wicker, with these lovely teal cushions that she found on sale—and I listened to the voicemail, fully intending to call her right back after I finished my cup of tea. But I think what bothers me the most is my husband’s schedule. And it is not just the volunteer work, it is right here in my own home. My daughter, bless her, she means well, she really does. I have this lovely lavender body wash—my niece Sarah bought it for me from one of those fancy boutique shops downtown, the ones where everything costs an arm and a leg, but oh, it smells just divine, like a real English garden. doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a history of a specific acquired brain injury, which would support F02.8 or F09 over primary Alzheimer disease.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of stroke, head injury, or other neurological problems to rule out medical causes for the symptoms, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, thank goodness. Nothing like that at all. I have never had a stroke or a brain injury or anything of that dreadful sort. I've always been very healthy in that regard. 

Well, I did have a terrible bout of vertigo once, oh, it must have been in the late nineties. The room would just spin and spin every time I turned my head too quickly. It was awful, truly awful. I had to sleep propped up on three pillows for a fortnight. Dr. Miller—he was our physician back then, before he retired and moved to Florida, lovely man with the most calming bedside manner—he said it was an inner ear thing. But that wasn't my brain, you see. That was just my ears acting up. 

But as for actual brain problems, like a stroke? No, I've never had anything like that. My mother, rest her soul, she had a small stroke when she was eighty-two, and it affected her speech for a little while. She couldn't find the right words for things. She kept calling the refrigerator the "cold box," which we all thought was rather sweet, but it was very frightening at the time. So I know what that looks like, and I haven't had anything even remotely similar. 

I've never fallen and hit my head, either. I'm very careful about that. I always hold the handrail when I go down the stairs to the basement, even when I'm carrying a load of laundry, which is getting harder to do these days. I make sure to leave one hand free just for the rail. And I wear sensible shoes around the house, none of those slippery slippers that can send you flying across the linoleum. So no, my brain has never been injured or damaged in any physical way, it's just... well, it's just this dreadful fog and confusion with keeping everything organized lately. But physically? No, my brain has been perfectly fine.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose... yes, I think they have been getting steadily worse, though it’s hard to put an exact finger on when it really started going downhill. It’s not like waking up one morning and suddenly everything is different, you know? It’s more like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it at first, but then one day you realize you're driving on the rim. 

I mean, I look back to maybe five or six years ago, and I was still juggling so many things. I’d have the church bake sale on a Tuesday, my book club on Thursday, and I’d still manage to remember to send out all the grandchildren’s birthday cards right on time, with a crisp five-dollar bill tucked inside. But then, little by little, the edges started fraying. First, it was just walking into a room and forgetting why I went in there, which everyone does, right? I used to joke with my neighbor, Susan—she lives in the blue house at the end of the cul-de-sac, lovely woman, makes the most incredible rhubarb pie—I used to joke with her that my brain was just too full of recipes and old phone numbers to fit anything new. 

But then it wasn't a joke anymore. It progressed from forgetting why I went into the kitchen to forgetting to pay the electric bill for two months in a row. And then the auction incident I told you about... that was the real wake-up call. It just feels like every year, every month even, the fog gets a little thicker.
